title: The coffee run: a person, the scripted baseline and the chance floor
question: How does a person's coffee run compare with an agent's on what the world can measure for both: time, route, collisions and coffee retained?
hypothesis: On the coffee run, the scripted baseline (smooth executor driving) retains more coffee than a person, while a person is faster; the random agent almost never delivers. This is a comparison of observable behaviour, not a contest: perception and motor control differ between the columns.

motivation.observation: The README says no human reference run is committed and that a side-by-side comparison is something you record yourself. Human sessions now record route samples, overshoots and the same windows as agents, so a person's exported trace can be imported into this experiment and compared on shared metrics only.
evidence: README.md: 'No human reference run is committed yet'
tests/agent-motor.test.ts: smooth vs aggressive driving, 100% vs 11% coffee

successCriteria: the random agent delivers far less often than the baseline (the floor is low)
falsificationCriteria: the random agent delivers as often as the baseline: the coffee run would not discriminate at all
limitations: Human runs are recorded in the browser and imported; their seeds are not controlled, so human comparisons are measurements only, never verdicts.
A person perceives pixels and audio and steers every frame; agents read text and use the shared executor. Only world-measured metrics are compared.
The random agent may choose 'hand control back', which ends its run: that is what the random provider does in the product too.
